sections.heading: Do not confuse this with franchise classification
paragraphs: A franchise inquiry examines the brand, operating control/assistance and payments. Joint-employer inquiries concern responsibilities for workers under their own laws. One relationship file may contain relevant facts for both, but a conclusion under one test does not establish the other. Keep each result and its limits visible in the operating plan.

learningSummary: A local operator may employ the team while a brand, customer or related company also influences the work. Joint-employer analysis asks whether more than one entity has responsibilities under a particular employment law. There is no single test that answers every law—or the separate franchise-definition question. The FLSA proposal is not an effective rule, and this guide does not supply a full governing-court or state-law determination.

seoTitle: Product safety: certification, eFiling and reporting

sections.heading: Identify the actual product and intended users
paragraphs: The consumer-product definition and exclusions require a factual scope check. Identify the article, ordinary users, intended use, materials and other agencies potentially involved. Neither a business customer nor an equipment label alone answers that legal question.

This guide covers the CPSC certification/reporting pathway. It does not determine an electrical, machinery, food, pesticide or workplace standard for an unidentified product. Keep those specific questions assigned rather than marking an entire import file product-safe.

sections.heading: Assign certification to a named responsible party
paragraphs: For covered imported finished products, Part 1110 defines the importer/certifier role, certificate contents and eFiling process. It permits specified broker/owner/purchaser/consignee allocations, while the identified certifier remains legally responsible for validity, accuracy, completeness and availability.

Identify the actual rules and testing basis. A bought template does not demonstrate that the product satisfies them. The part also includes five-year supporting-record requirements and conditions for access/furnishing. Give those records an owner distinct from the logistics booking contact if necessary.

sections.heading: Use the real phase dates and distinguish enforcement policy
paragraphs: The final action makes the requirements effective July 8, 2026 for most covered products. Specified FTZ entries have a January 8, 2027 phase, still future at the existing November 2026 review. Do not apply one date to every entry.

CPSC’s FAQ describes an initial policy of not seeking entry denial solely for missing eFiling data while continuing certificate enforcement. That is an enforcement description, not an exemption, guaranteed entry outcome or permission to ignore applicable safety rules. It is also time-sensitive and should not be treated as permanent grace.

sections.heading: Give complaint escalation a separate reporting route
paragraphs: Covered firms can have an immediate reporting duty when information reasonably supports the specified noncompliance, a potentially substantial product hazard or an unreasonable serious-injury/death risk (15 U.S. Code § 2064(b)). The timing rule interprets immediate as 24 hours with its weekend/holiday computation, and warns against waiting for complete risk estimates (§ 1115.14).

A reasonable investigation is not automatic permission to delay once reportable information is known. Identify who receives complaints, preserves evidence and makes prompt escalation possible. A supplier’s promise to handle the issue does not settle every other entity’s duty.

sections.heading: Fictional example: certification does not close a safety complaint
paragraphs: A brand has an import certificate file for a consumer product and later receives information about overheating. The product lead preserves the complaint and available facts and routes them for the actual reporting-threshold assessment. The earlier certificate is not used as a reason to ignore new information.

The team records the product, applicable standard, certifier, evidence and reporting owner. It does not assume a recall, reportable defect or shipment clearance from this example. Unverified tests, technical standards, fees and other authorisations stay unresolved until supported.

The internal escalation owner is a practical business assignment, not a new statutory office. The purpose is to bring the actual information promptly to the reporting assessment rather than wait for a complete risk estimate by default. Product scope, technical standards and the time-sensitive eFiling policy still need their respective checks; no recall, report or entry outcome follows from the table.

The cited rule interprets immediate as 24 hours with its computation qualifications.

A B 2 B invoice or branded label does not settle jurisdiction. Certification and reporting serious safety information are separate responsibilities. The eFiling policy is time-sensitive, and this guide does not establish product scope, a test result or a reportable complaint.

seoTitle: Overseas data access: DOJ scope, thresholds and limits

sections.heading: Map who can see the data, not just where it is stored
paragraphs: The first screen identifies the U.S. person, foreign/covered person, data, volume and agreement. Remote support access can matter even when no file is downloaded or the database stays in the United States. Conversely, a foreign address alone does not establish a prohibited transaction.

Part 202’s countries-of-concern and covered-person definitions have their own ownership, organisation, employment, primary-residence and designation rules. The recorded list names China, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Russia and Venezuela, with China’s stated Hong Kong/Macau definition. Citizenship alone or an OFAC name result is not the complete test; an unlisted entity can meet a defined category.

sections.heading: Use the exact counts and aggregation period
paragraphs: Government-related data has specified regardless-of-volume criteria. Bulk U.S. sensitive personal data uses category-specific thresholds and the preceding 12 months with the specified same-party conditions. A new invoice does not reset the total.

The table preserves the rule’s “more than” comparisons and its distinction between persons and devices. Mixed datasets have their own rule and need separate assessment. These counts do not provide a safe harbour for government-related data or other privacy laws.

sections.heading: Separate prohibited, restricted and exempt arrangements
paragraphs: Data brokerage and specified human-omic transactions have prohibitions. Relevant vendor, employment and investment transactions can be restricted, subject to the actual security and other conditions. Restricted transactions require the current diligence programme and annual audit conditions.

There is a bounded exemption for corporate-group administrative/ancillary operations. An ordinary independent franchise or licence partner is not assumed to be a qualifying subsidiary or affiliate. Identify the exact exemption and facts rather than treating all brand-network activity as internal. Do not replace prescribed security requirements with controls the company merely regards as equivalent.

paragraphs: A U.S. operator proposes overseas helpdesk access to its system. The project team first records what the user can view or edit, which data categories and volumes are involved, the parties’ relevant status and the contract. It does not conclude that storage in the United States removes the access question.

The reviewer then assesses whether a defined transaction, prohibition, restriction or supported exemption applies. This example authorises no account. Detailed CISA technical security requirements were not read through the access-blocked resource in the existing review, so those implementation questions remain explicit.

The table is a sequence of questions, not a points test. Clearing one question does not clear the rest, and the earlier threshold table does not supply a general privacy safe harbour. Preserve the recorded October 5/October 6 source difference and apply the cited operative provisions rather than silently choosing a new date.

paragraphs: The programme took effect April 8, 2025. The operative diligence/audit provisions use October 6, 2025. The DOJ overview’s October 5 wording is a recorded source difference; the guide follows §§ 202.1001–1002 and the implementation policy.

DOJ’s old good-faith enforcement-priority policy ran only through July 8, 2025 and is not continuing grace. Build a data/actor/access/agreement matrix and assign actual controls and reporting questions before access depends on approval. Keep personal data in authorised systems outside this site and assess other U.S., origin-country, sector, contractual and privacy obligations separately.

Part 202 asks a specific national-security question about defined parties, data and transactions—not whether every overseas connection is automatically forbidden. Detailed CISA implementation requirements remain unresolved in this review, so a scope assessment is not account authorisation.

seoTitle: Franchise vs licensing in the U.S.: the federal inquiry

sections.heading: The business decision comes before the contract label
paragraphs: An established company may want local owners to find customers, employ staff and deliver its service under a common brand. Licensing sounds like a simple description of that plan. The legal question is broader: are you only allowing use of a protected name, or supplying a business method that the local owner will follow?

The U.S. Federal Trade Commission’s Franchise Rule examines a continuing commercial relationship involving trademark association, significant control or assistance over the operating method, and a required payment or commitment. Consider the three elements together. Describing the partner as an investor, distributor or licensee does not decide whether those facts are present.

sections.heading: Keep the definition and an exemption separate
paragraphs: First describe the relationship. Then examine whether a federal exclusion or exemption applies. An exemption has its own conditions; it is not a reason to omit inconvenient facts from the description. A federal conclusion also leaves independent state rules to examine. Different state definitions or sales requirements can produce additional work.

The useful management document is therefore a factual account, not a declaration that the model is “not a franchise.” Include the support promised in presentations and ordinary practice as well as the signed contract. Record payments to related companies too.

sections.heading: Fictional example: a maintenance brand builds a partner system
paragraphs: A European maintenance company proposes branded vans, a licence fee, mandatory scheduling software, initial training and required inspection methods. Its sales director initially treats these as separate purchases. Read together, however, they describe how the partner will operate the service.

The reviewer asks what the training covers, how much discretion the partner keeps, what the software controls and which payments are unavoidable. Software alone does not settle the test. Separating the licence, training and software charges into three invoices does not remove the need to examine them together. The next step is to establish the facts, not to announce a legal result.

This is the starting page for the complete federal relationship inquiry. The support, payment-exemption and single-license guides answer narrower questions after the facts are assembled. Splitting invoices or changing the contract heading does not remove the need to examine those facts together.

paragraphs: Ask operations to describe delivery requirements, finance to map payments, and the expansion lead to identify the parties and locations. Keep unresolved answers visible.

seoTitle: Significant control or assistance in a franchise system

sections.heading: Why ordinary support creates a legal question
paragraphs: A foreign brand may regard training and software as helpful extras. A new U.S. operator may rely on them to price jobs, allocate staff, win customers and deliver the service. That reliance helps explain why the federal inquiry considers the whole operating method rather than asking whether the contract includes a manual.

The definition addresses significant control or assistance. The brand’s right to impose controls matters as well as controls it has already exercised. Pre-contract promises and routine help also belong in the review; an incomplete contract summary can miss much of the actual system.

sections.heading: Distinguish protecting the name from directing the business
paragraphs: The FTC’s May 2008 Compliance Guide gives explanatory examples such as training, accounting systems, management advice and detailed manuals. It discusses the operator’s reasonable reliance and the overall method of operation. It is dated guidance, to be read with the current rule, not a current threshold sheet.

A requirement solely protecting legal ownership of a trademark differs from broader instructions about staffing, routes, sales methods or customer restrictions. Neither a logo guide nor a software subscription automatically decides the result. Ask what each requirement does in practice and how it connects to the rest of the system.

sections.heading: Fictional example: two different facilities-service documents
paragraphs: A facilities brand has a short logo guide specifying colours and approved use of its name. It also has a “quality appendix” covering which accounts operators accept, staffing levels, sales scripts, mandatory software, service reports and remedial visits.

The operations director explains each instruction’s purpose and supplies examples of support calls. The reviewer can then distinguish trademark protection from a wider operating system. Calling the second document an appendix does not reduce its importance. Equally, finding one detailed requirement is not a substitute for assessing the complete relationship.

Self-check: if no intervention has happened yet, can a contractual right to impose operating controls be left out? No. Include that right and promised assistance as well as actual conduct. The comparison helps explain the facts; it does not create a safe harbour for either document.

paragraphs: For each requirement, record who can change it, whether it is mandatory in practice, how the brand monitors it and what happens if the operator ignores it. This inventory is a preparation tool, not a separate legal filing.

seoTitle: The $735 franchise exemption: payments and commitments

sections.heading: Apply the current amount and time period
paragraphs: For this exemption, the total required payments or commitments to the franchisor or an affiliate must be less than $735, counting from before operations begin through six months after they commence. Exactly $735 is not less than $735. These are the amount and period in 16 CFR 436.8(a)(1).

This is an exemption from specified federal franchise disclosure requirements, not the universal definition of a franchise and not an exemption from state law. Assess the relationship’s brand, operating-control or assistance, and payment facts before treating the payment exemption as the answer to the entire legal question. Older material quoting $500 does not supply the current amount.

sections.heading: Read the commitment as well as the bank statement
paragraphs: Include required training, software, equipment, royalties and purchases from related companies where the rule’s payment definition reaches them. A fee can matter even before cash changes hands if the partner has made the relevant commitment to pay.

The required-payment definition has a specific exclusion for reasonable quantities of inventory bought at bona fide wholesale prices for resale or lease. It does not remove every supply purchase. A service company should not assume that equipment or materials used to deliver its service automatically fall within an inventory-for-resale exclusion.

sections.heading: Fictional example: a fee split into three parts
paragraphs: A brand proposes a $300 initial fee and requires a $250 training payment and a $250 software commitment to its affiliate within the relevant period. Assuming all three are required payments within the rule, the total is $800. Looking only at the $300 initial invoice would miss the relevant total.

The brand then suggests collecting the software money later. Finance still needs to show when the obligation is undertaken, not merely the proposed collection date. The reviewer must decide the actual treatment from the agreement and business facts; this illustration does not establish an exemption for a real transaction.

Self-check: would exactly $735 satisfy this amount condition? No: the comparison is less than $735, not $735 or less. Moving a collection date does not establish that the payment commitment moved. In a real schedule, leave an unpriced required purchase unknown until its amount and treatment are established; do not enter zero to make the total fit.

seoTitle: Single trademark licence: licensees, outlets and future grants

sections.heading: Start with the complete licensing plan
paragraphs: The FTC Compliance Guide describes a narrow exclusion for a single licensee using a trademark. That description is not one free franchise, one free outlet, or one licence in every state. A brand’s existing grants and intended later grants therefore matter.

Do not isolate the first signed contract from the planned network. The reviewer needs to know what rights have been granted, who holds them and what the brand expects to grant next. Separate state rules remain a question even if the narrow federal treatment is available.

sections.heading: Understand what the historical opinion can establish
paragraphs: FTC staff opinion 05-1, dated January 5, 2005, addressed a particular salon arrangement using an earlier rule citation. Staff expressly said that its view was not binding on the Commission. Its discussion distinguishes licensees from outlets and notes that intended future licences would change the analysis.

The opinion helps identify relevant questions. It does not give today’s applicant a ruling simply because its proposal also involves a salon or one initial contract. The May 2008 guide is explanatory material too; the historical dates and limited authority should remain clear when using it.

sections.heading: Fictional example: “exclusive” rights in three states
paragraphs: A European service brand proposes a Texas licence for Company A, a California licence for Company B and an Illinois licence for Company C. Each agreement says the local company is the sole licensee in its state. There are nevertheless three proposed licensees in the overall plan. State-by-state exclusivity does not turn that plan into a single-license arrangement.

Conversely, counting buildings alone can be misleading where a single licensee runs several outlets. That distinction is a reason to obtain a complete factual review, not a conclusion that any multi-outlet arrangement qualifies.

The register counts actual legal entities, not trading names or state labels. Its purpose is to let the reviewer ask the precise single-license question using the complete plan. The nonbinding, fact-specific 2005 opinion is not a current approval simply because the applicant also starts with one agreement.

seoTitle: State franchise sales: map buyer, seller and offer locations

sections.heading: Why one outlet address is not enough
paragraphs: Federal disclosure and state franchise-sales rules are separate layers. The federal rule preserves state and local franchise-practices laws except to the extent of inconsistency; equal or greater protection is not inconsistent. A federal disclosure process therefore does not replace the state analysis.

The relevant state questions can involve the seller’s location, the buyer’s residence, the operating location, and where communications originate or are received. This guide identifies facts to collect. It does not assert that every one of those connections triggers every state law.

sections.heading: Describe what happens before the final agreement
paragraphs: A recruitment process may include website advertising, broker introductions, discovery meetings, territory discussions, disclosure, deposits and signing. Those steps should not be reduced to a single proposed opening date. What the communication contains, where the people are, and whether money or a binding promise arises can change the review.

There is no universal prohibition on introductory calls stated here. The useful question is what this particular call or document proposes and which applicable law governs it. Similarly, an internal spreadsheet saying “registration complete” should identify the actual state, entity, offering and evidence.

sections.heading: Fictional example: New York buyer, Florida operation
paragraphs: A Singapore parent speaks with a prospective partner who lives in New York about a Florida operation. A U.S. subsidiary will sell the rights, and a broker introduces the parties. A worksheet containing only “Florida outlet” leaves important facts out.

The expansion lead adds each entity’s identity, each participant’s location, the proposed communications, the intended contracting party and any deposit. The reviewer can then examine the relevant state connections and exemptions. The example does not decide that a particular New York or Florida filing is required; it shows why a fuller map is needed before that decision.

The map does not prove that every listed place triggers a filing. It separates the facts needed to examine each jurisdiction from the eventual conclusion under its law. Use the state guides for the named questions, and keep actual operating permissions in additional checks.

paragraphs: Create a table with a row for each potentially relevant jurisdiction. Keep classification, registration, notice, exemption, disclosure, advertising and continuing relationship rules in separate columns. These terms ask different questions: whether the model is covered, whether a filing is needed, what information must be given, and how the relationship is regulated.

Assign a named person and supporting document to each conclusion. A blank means unresearched, not no requirement. Retain the facts and reasoning supporting any conclusion that a rule does not apply. Operational permits and other local business obligations belong in additional checks.

seoTitle: FDD disclosure timing: agreements, deposits and delivery

sections.heading: Understand the federal waiting period
paragraphs: For a covered, nonexempt franchise to be located in the United States or its territories, the current FDD generally must be furnished at least 14 calendar days before the prospective franchisee signs a binding agreement with, or makes payment to, the franchisor or an affiliate in connection with the proposed sale. An affiliate is a related company.

Both agreement and payment matter. Moving a charge to a related company does not by itself remove the payment question. Nor should the team assume that money falls outside the review merely because it is called a reservation or can be refunded.

sections.heading: Find the first commitment in the actual sales process
paragraphs: Work backwards from every proposed binding document or payment, not only the final franchise agreement. A territory reservation, preliminary agreement or deposit may occur earlier. Record what each document actually commits the parties to and why each payment is requested.

Keep the document version and exhibits furnished to this prospect. Section 436.2 specifies delivery methods, including particular treatment for mailing. Choose a permitted method and have the counting and delivery evidence checked. An educational website visit or a tick beside a training module is not evidence that the required FDD was furnished.

sections.heading: Fictional example: the deposit comes first
paragraphs: A Dutch industrial-services brand expects to sign a franchise agreement near the end of a month. Its sales manager asks the candidate to pay a territory deposit earlier so another applicant cannot take the area. The manager has calculated the disclosure timetable only from the final signing date.

The disclosure coordinator adds the deposit request to the timetable and sends its terms for review. If it is a relevant payment, the waiting period must be satisfied before that earlier event. Postponing the final signature would not cure a premature payment. The team checks state requirements and any later agreement changes separately; this example does not decide the treatment of a particular reservation.

Self-check: if the team has allowed 14 calendar days before final signing, has it necessarily checked the proposed earlier deposit? No. It must identify the relevant event and establish the permitted delivery and counting facts. This sequence supplies no legal treatment for a particular reservation and no invented delivery date.

paragraphs: The log is an internal control supporting the legal delivery obligation. A named person should check the earliest agreement/payment date before sales staff ask for either.

seoTitle: Revised franchise agreements: the seven-day trigger

sections.heading: The seven-day requirement has a particular trigger
paragraphs: A franchisor that unilaterally and materially changes the attached basic franchise agreement or related agreements must furnish each revised agreement at least seven calendar days before it is signed. This revised-agreement requirement sits alongside the general FDD disclosure period (16 CFR 436.2(b)).

It is not a rule that every edit restarts every clock. First establish whether the change is material, whether it is unilateral and which agreement has changed. The exact revised documents and proposed signature date matter.

sections.heading: Keep prospect-initiated negotiations distinguishable
paragraphs: The text treats changes arising from negotiations initiated by the prospective franchisee differently: those changes do not trigger this particular seven-day period. That distinction requires facts. Calling a change “negotiated” in the file is not enough if the franchisor proposed it.

Record the request, the earlier wording, the proposed wording and its commercial effect. Keep emails or meeting notes showing who raised the issue. A clean final agreement helps signing, but a marked comparison helps the reviewer understand whether the timing rule applies. State amendment or further-disclosure requirements remain separate.

sections.heading: Fictional example: two changes with different histories
paragraphs: After providing its FDD, a brand decides all new operators must pay a new field-support charge. The prospect did not request it. The team preserves the old and new provisions and asks whether this is a unilateral material change requiring revised-agreement delivery and the seven-calendar-day period. An informal sales assurance cannot answer that question.

In the same transaction, the prospect asks to alter a territory boundary during negotiations. That change has a different origin. The file should show the request and negotiations rather than combine both changes under one label. Neither example supplies a universal materiality ruling or decides state-law requirements.

The marked comparison explains what changed; the request or decision record explains who initiated it. Neither alone establishes every materiality or state-law answer. Keep the general FDD timetable and independent state amendment or disclosure questions alongside this narrower revised-agreement review.

paragraphs: The reviewer determines the legal effect and timing. Sales prevents premature signatures and payment requests under the applicable process. Operations confirms whether revised support promises can actually be performed.

seoTitle: FDD updates and records: annual, quarterly and retention duties

sections.heading: Use separate annual and quarterly clocks
paragraphs: The federal rule requires a revised FDD within 120 days after the end of the fiscal year, followed by distribution of only the revised document. It also calls for quarterly revisions within a reasonable time after quarter-end for material changes. Do not convert “reasonable time” into an invented fixed number of days.

Known material changes in Item 19 information must be communicated when the FDD is furnished. That specific requirement needs its own check; waiting for the next annual revision is not a complete approach to changing performance information. State renewals and amendments also need separate calendars.

sections.heading: Collect changes from the people who know them
paragraphs: Finance holds statements, fee information and financial-performance data. Operations knows about training, suppliers, personnel and support arrangements. Development maintains outlet information. The person managing disputes and agreements knows about changes that other teams may not see.

Create a simple intake record stating what happened, when, which disclosure it may affect and who will assess it. A team member reports the business fact; the responsible reviewer decides the disclosure consequence. Keep those roles distinct rather than expecting every manager to make a legal materiality decision.

sections.heading: Fictional example: support is outsourced mid-year
paragraphs: A French service brand transfers U.S. field support to a contractor after delivering its annual FDD. The operations lead records the new provider, changed personnel, service commitments and relevant contractual wording. The disclosure owner compares those facts with what prospects have been told.

The issue is not whether the next brochure looks outdated. It is whether assistance or other required information has materially changed, which updates or communications are needed, and which prospects received an earlier version. The team records that assessment while continuing to maintain its separate state filing calendar.

A team member reports the business event; the responsible reviewer assesses its disclosure effect. These are practical internal assignments, not a requirement that every manager decide legal materiality. The specific Item 19 communication duty and the distinct retention descriptions below remain separate checks.

paragraphs: The federal rule requires materially different FDD versions to be kept for three years after the close of the fiscal year in which each was last used (§ 436.6(h)). Signed receipts for completed sales must be kept for at least three years (§ 436.6(i)). These are different retention descriptions.

Use a controlled repository with a named owner. Preserve the actual files furnished, their use dates and the matching prospect records. Replacing an old file with an edited document of the same name destroys the ability to explain what was disclosed at the time.

These rows are not one universal deletion date. Keep the actual record category and the rule’s own description; do not make the FDD version disappear merely because a different transaction record has reached an assumed retention date.

seoTitle: Home-market revenue in U.S. franchise earnings claims

sections.heading: A claim can appear in a spreadsheet or conversation
paragraphs: The federal definition reaches oral, written and visual statements and mathematical calculations. A slide, calculator result, message or spoken answer can therefore matter as well as a formal forecast. Calling a figure illustrative does not itself decide its legal treatment.

An internal planning model has a different audience from a recruitment presentation. Before sending it to prospects, examine what it represents and whether the required basis, supporting documents and disclosure conditions are satisfied. The franchisor should also control what brokers and other sellers say.

sections.heading: Answer Item 19 even when choosing not to make a claim
paragraphs: A franchisor may elect not to make a financial performance representation, but it must still answer Item 19 with the required negative disclosure. Where a representation is made, a reasonable basis, written substantiation and the item’s requirements matter.

There is defined treatment for specific-outlet records and compliant supplemental representations. Those are conditional routes, not permission to give any figures privately. Have the exact proposed statement and supporting material reviewed before relying on an exception or supplement.

sections.heading: Fictional example: $1 million of Singapore cleaning revenue
paragraphs: A Singapore cleaning outlet reports annual revenue equivalent to US$1 million. The brand wants to put that figure beside a U.S. territory map. Finance can verify the currency conversion, but that does not establish what a U.S. operator will sell or retain as profit.

The reader needs to understand the operating period, customer mix, included outlets and whether costs are omitted. U.S. management pay, insurance, collections and local sales costs may differ. Selecting one strong outlet may also give a misleading picture of the wider group. The reviewer therefore examines the proposed claim, relevant data and material differences, rather than approving a headline because its arithmetic is correct.

The second use changes the audience and surrounding message, not the underlying Singapore accounts. The team must assess the actual claim and its applicable treatment. This comparison supplies neither an approved U.S. forecast nor compliant replacement wording; the advertising guide addresses live versions, while Item 19 explains the disclosure content.

seoTitle: Area development vs master franchising: roles and costs

sections.heading: Separate delivering services from supporting business owners
paragraphs: An own-unit operator recruits staff, wins customers and delivers the service through its business. An area developer adds an agreed development programme for its own units. A master arrangement can add independent-owner recruitment, disclosure, contracting, training, support and disputes. Those are additional jobs, not simply a larger sales territory.

Titles vary. Distribution and intellectual-property licensing also require their own analysis of goods, payments and controls. A contract heading cannot establish who performs the work or which legal rules apply.

sections.heading: Why the intermediary’s role matters legally
paragraphs: An intermediary can fall within the federal franchisor definition as a subfranchisor when it engages in both pre-sale activities and post-sale performance (§ 436.1(k)). Identify the actual conduct rather than assuming only the foreign brand has responsibilities. Item 21 also specifies separate subfranchisor financial statements in the relevant arrangement.

A role allocation helps explain who does what, but does not erase regulatory duties. Keep three diagrams if necessary: who contracts with whom, where the money goes, and who provides operating support. They may show different relationships.

sections.heading: Fictional example: four managed branches are not yet a network
paragraphs: A French industrial-maintenance operator successfully manages four branches. It proposes recruiting independent U.S. owners under a master agreement. Its existing evidence shows that it can train employees and serve customers, but it has no franchise-sales process or dedicated owner-support team.

The brand compares two plans. An own-unit development plan builds on current delivery capability. A subfranchise plan requires additional people, sales controls, disclosure records and ongoing support funding. This is a commercial capability comparison, not a recommendation that one legal structure is available or preferable for the actual parties.

In the fictional four-branch example, success with employees and customers supports one kind of capability. It does not establish an owner-recruitment process or funded support for independent franchisees. Follow the contracts, money and work in separate diagrams if needed; the actual conduct, rather than the title in this comparison, controls the relevant legal questions.

seoTitle: Foreign audits for the FDD: entities, GAAP and audit scope

sections.heading: Treat preparation and audit as two questions
paragraphs: Item 21 specifies financial statements prepared under U.S. generally accepted accounting principles, commonly called U.S. GAAP, or principles permitted by the Securities and Exchange Commission, and the applicable U.S. generally accepted auditing standards. Having an audit does not by itself answer either question.

The FTC’s May 2008 explanatory guide discusses foreign accounting, but its age matters. The responsible auditor should confirm current SEC-permitted treatment rather than reading that guide as blanket acceptance of any accounts prepared under International Financial Reporting Standards. Identify the proposed basis and audit approach expressly.

sections.heading: Map the promises before choosing the accounts
paragraphs: The company selling U.S. franchise rights may be a new subsidiary rather than the foreign parent. The group may nevertheless promise that the parent will train operators, provide support or guarantee obligations. Subfranchisor roles can add further financial-disclosure questions.

Give the reviewer the actual agreements and guarantees, not only an organisation chart. A thin selling subsidiary does not make the parent’s promises disappear. Conversely, the existence of a strong parent does not automatically permit the subsidiary simply to attach the parent’s annual report.

sections.heading: Fictional example: the parent supplies the support
paragraphs: A European group forms a U.S. company to sell franchises. Its presentations say the European parent will train every new operator and provide technical support. Finance initially budgets only for the subsidiary’s opening accounts.

The CFO collects the support wording, any guarantees and the proposed contracts. The reviewer and auditor identify the relevant entities, reporting dates, preparation basis and audit work. If reconciliation or additional statements are needed, that affects the timetable. The example identifies a preparation gap; it does not decide the exact statements required for that group.

The proposed scope makes unanswered questions visible; it does not approve the existing accounts. Which companies supply statements, how the statements are prepared and how they are audited are three separate questions. Current acceptance, startup-phase-in eligibility and state financial-assurance treatment remain unresolved for the actual group.

paragraphs: Ask the auditor for a work plan stating which entities and periods are covered, the accounting and audit standards, any reconciliation approach and the expected delivery date. Coordinate that plan with the actual disclosure schedule.

The federal startup phase-in has conditions. It is not a universal shortcut for an established foreign system and does not establish acceptance under state rules. Financial-assurance questions also need their own review. seoTitle: U.S. royalties abroad: withholding, net cash and gross-up

sections.heading: Start with the payment and recipient
paragraphs: The Internal Revenue Service describes a general 30% withholding regime for many types of U.S.-source income paid to foreign persons. Statutory or treaty relief may reduce the result, depending on the facts and documentation. This is not a statement that every cross-border payment bears 30%.

Ask first what the payment is for, where the relevant income is sourced, who receives and beneficially owns it, and whether the claimed relief applies. Incorporation in a treaty country or a company address is not a complete treaty analysis. Applicable conditions and limitation provisions need their own review.

sections.heading: Show three cash lines instead of one royalty headline
paragraphs: The budget should display the contractual gross royalty, the amount withheld and remitted, and the cash received by the foreign brand. If the agreement contains a gross-up, model its effect on the payer’s cost rather than assuming the written royalty is the whole expense.

This is useful business planning alongside the tax analysis. The applicable rate stays an assumption until reviewed. An unknown rate should not silently become zero in a forecast, particularly when the brand is relying on royalty receipts to fund training and support.

sections.heading: Fictional example: sensitivity, not a treaty quotation
paragraphs: Assume an annual gross royalty of US$100,000 and a hypothetical 10% withholding rate solely to examine cash sensitivity. The payer withholds US$10,000, leaving US$90,000 for the foreign brand before support costs. The example does not identify an actual treaty rate for any country.

If the commercial plan had allocated the full US$100,000 to overseas support, it would now have a funding gap. Finance must resolve the actual rate, documentation and any gross-up terms before treating the support budget as funded. Correct arithmetic cannot establish entitlement to treaty relief.

For the second row only, assume the contract promises the brand a net US$100,000 after this hypothetical 10% deduction and no other adjustment. Dividing US$100,000 by 0.90 shows the illustrative gross amount; the displayed figures are rounded. This demonstrates a possible gross-up effect, not an actual treaty rate or interpretation of any contract. The payer’s cost and the brand’s support cash must each be modelled under the real terms.

seoTitle: FinCEN BOI: U.S.-created versus foreign-formed companies

sections.heading: Foreign ownership and foreign formation ask different questions
paragraphs: As recorded in the November 12, 2026 review, 31 CFR 1010.380 exempts U.S.-created domestic entities. A nonexempt entity formed abroad and registered by filing in a U.S. state or tribal jurisdiction can remain a reporting company. The owners’ nationality alone does not answer which branch applies.

Read the entity’s formation record and the actual registration filing. A group may contain both a U.S.-created subsidiary and a foreign parent registered separately. A conclusion about one company is not automatically a conclusion about every company in the group.

sections.heading: Use the narrowed rule and the relevant notice date
paragraphs: FinCEN’s final rule effective August 14, 2026 preserves the narrowed scope and provides specified relief for U.S.-person beneficial-owner and company-applicant information. Older 2024 or early-2025 checklists can describe superseded duties. Do not ask for documents merely because a historic checklist includes them.

For new in-scope reporting companies on or after March 26, 2025, the recorded rule uses 30 calendar days from the earlier actual or public registration notice, subject to applicable relief. Identify both possible notice events rather than starting from an informal internal announcement. Check current exemptions and any applicable judicial or agency relief at the filing date.

sections.heading: Fictional example: two Malaysian expansion structures
paragraphs: In one plan, a Malaysian company creates a new U.S. subsidiary. In another, it registers the Malaysian entity itself to do business in a state. The first plan involves a U.S.-created entity; the second involves a foreign-formed entity and a U.S. registration event.

The company secretary records those differences and asks whether the foreign registration is in scope or covered by another exemption. The subsidiary’s domestic exemption does not decide a separate parent registration. Neither example determines the actual company’s complete reporting or tax position.

This comparison applies the scope recorded in the November 2026 review; it is not a new legal update. Do not substitute foreign-owned for foreign-formed. Keep the entity’s BOI decision separate from IRS returns, state annual reports, banking and sanctions checks, and retain sensitive documents only in the authorised private process.

seoTitle: BE-13 reporting: new foreign investment and exemption claims

sections.heading: Identify what the foreign group is doing
paragraphs: The current BEA decision tree distinguishes buying a business, establishing a new U.S. entity and expanding an existing investment. Formation can be relevant even before physical operations begin. Begin with the actual transaction rather than looking for one threshold that answers every situation.

The CFO should document the parties, ownership and voting interests, event date and relevant costs. That factual file helps select the form and determine whether a full report or an exemption claim is required. Do not wait for the first customer invoice before asking the question.

sections.heading: The acquisition threshold is not a universal exemption
paragraphs: The BE-13A revision 10/2025 linked in the recorded review uses an acquisition cost greater than US$40 million together with a foreign voting-interest condition. It is an acquisition form, not the form for every establishment or expansion. Older instructions can show different amounts.

A transaction below a full-report threshold can still require a Claim for Exemption. Therefore “below US$40 million” does not mean “no BEA filing.” Read the current form instructions for the selected branch, including the applicable ownership conditions, rather than transferring one number across the whole survey.

sections.heading: Fictional example: a modest service startup
paragraphs: A Singapore services group creates a U.S. entity with a modest startup budget and no premises yet. Its management assumes it can ignore investment surveys because it has not bought a factory. The finance lead instead records that this is an establishment proposal, the group’s voting and equity interests, and expected costs.

The preparer follows the establishment branch and determines the applicable report or exemption claim. The group does not use the acquisition form’s cost threshold to close a different question. The illustration identifies the process; it does not select a form for an actual investment.

Self-check: does below US$40 million close the reporting question for this establishment? No. The reviewed greater-than-US$40-million acquisition condition belongs to BE-13A with its stated ownership condition. A different branch needs its own review, and a required Claim for Exemption is a response rather than doing nothing.

seoTitle: Form 5472: foreign-owned LLC reporting before revenue

sections.heading: Understand the separate information-return question
paragraphs: The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Form 5472 instructions include certain foreign-owned U.S. disregarded entities in the reporting framework and describe special mechanics using a pro forma Form 1120. Filing depends on the reporting-corporation rules, reportable transactions and exceptions.

Do not replace that analysis with “the LLC has one member” or “there is no taxable profit.” Ordinary income-tax classification and information reporting ask different questions. The preparer needs to identify the relevant entity and transactions before deciding what must be filed.

sections.heading: Record money movements before customers arrive
paragraphs: Keep evidence of capital contributions, distributions, loans, royalties, intercompany charges and nonmonetary transactions. These records let the preparer decide what the instructions reach; the list does not declare that every entry has identical treatment.

An early transfer may be described casually as “startup cash” while the documents describe a loan or ownership contribution. Resolve that description in the records instead of leaving the preparer to infer it from a bank balance months later. Preserve the actual counterparties and dates.

sections.heading: Fictional example: a funded but dormant startup
paragraphs: A foreign parent forms a wholly owned U.S. LLC and transfers funds for anticipated expenses. The LLC has no customer revenue at year-end. Its manager assumes there is no reporting work because trading has not started.

The tax preparer asks for the formation documents, ownership, funding agreement and transfer record. Those facts are needed to assess reportable transactions and special filing mechanics. No revenue does not establish that there were no relevant transactions. The example does not conclude which return the particular LLC owes; it explains why the funding record must reach the preparer.

Calling a transfer startup cash is not a complete transaction description. Give the preparer the actual agreement and money movement without declaring every item reportable. The optional record supports the analysis; it does not establish a return, deadline, exception or penalty for the LLC.

seoTitle: L-1 company relationships: a licence is not ownership proof

sections.heading: Start with the proposed work, not founder relocation
paragraphs: A brand owner can plan U.S. partner-operated expansion while remaining abroad. If local partners employ the team and deliver the service, founder relocation need not be assumed. If executives, trainers or technical staff will physically work in the United States, record the intended duties, place and duration early.

That work plan can affect launch feasibility. It should reach the relevant reviewer before operations depend on the person’s presence, rather than being treated as travel administration after the commercial agreement is signed.

sections.heading: A licence is not the required ownership evidence
paragraphs: An L-1 review covers a qualifying parent, branch, affiliate or subsidiary relationship, continuing business and evidence about the individual’s overseas employment and U.S. role (8 CFR 214.2(l)). Draw ownership percentages and voting/control rights separately from the brand-licensing arrangement.

A contract allowing one business to use another’s name does not alone prove the prescribed relationship. Equally, an organisation chart without supporting rights and employment evidence is not a complete individual case. New-office situations require additional evidence.

sections.heading: Fictional example: an unrelated U.S. partner
paragraphs: A German brand licenses an independently owned U.S. operator and wants its COO to run that operator’s business. The parties have a strong commercial relationship, but the licence does not establish common ownership and control.

The reviewer asks who owns and controls each entity, whether a prescribed corporate relationship exists, and what the COO actually did abroad and would do in the United States. Brand standards and a management title do not fill those gaps. This example does not decide the person’s eligibility or propose an alternative immigration route.

Think of two different diagrams: one shows permission to use the brand, and the other shows who owns and controls the companies. They may connect different parties and do different jobs. The staff-transfer guide addresses the person’s history, duties and organisation; neither diagram alone completes that assessment.

seoTitle: E-2 nationality: trace owners beyond a treaty-country company

sections.heading: Look through the company address
paragraphs: The E regulation directs nationality to be traced, as practicable, to the individuals who ultimately own the enterprise. It separately addresses investment, control, developing and directing the enterprise, and employee roles. Establishing a subsidiary in a treaty country does not itself answer those questions.

Keep the principal-investor and employee analyses distinct. Identify the proposed applicant and actual duties before treating an enterprise-level fact as the answer for a person. This is an eligibility review, not a recommendation to incorporate or invest in a particular country.

sections.heading: Read the treaty category and country footnotes
paragraphs: The State Department list distinguishes E-1 from E-2 and includes territorial and historical conditions. A country’s appearance in one category is not evidence of coverage in the other. The United Kingdom footnote, for example, includes nationality and inhabitant conditions.

Use the actual applicable entry and footnotes rather than a general “treaty country” label. A passport alone or a corporate address alone may leave relevant conditions unanswered. The country list also does not replace the regulation’s investment, ownership and role requirements.

sections.heading: Fictional example: Malaysian owners and a Singapore subsidiary
paragraphs: A Malaysian-owned group has a Singapore subsidiary and wants to build a U.S. franchise operation. Management initially assumes the Singapore registration makes the group eligible for E-2 treatment.

The reviewer instead needs the ownership chain through to individuals, control rights, the proposed applicant’s role and the committed investment. Those facts may produce questions that the registration certificate cannot answer. No conclusion about the actual group or any person follows from the example, and no passport upload is needed to prepare the initial ownership diagram.

Self-check: does the Singapore registration certificate let the team stop at the subsidiary? No. The nationality inquiry calls for the relevant ultimate-ownership tracing as practicable. It remains separate from tax residence, the applicant’s role and whether the actual investment meets its conditions.

seoTitle: PACER partner searches: identity, outcomes and limits

sections.heading: Understand the search’s geographical and court limits
paragraphs: PACER Case Locator indexes federal appellate, bankruptcy and district cases nationwide. It is not a complete index of state and local litigation. A blank federal search therefore does not prove that a company has never had a dispute.

Searches can also miss name variants or return a different business. Record legal names, relevant former names, search date and method. The result should be described as what the search found within its coverage, not as a general certificate of good conduct.

sections.heading: Read what happened, not just the case title
paragraphs: A complaint records allegations. A settlement, consent order, default judgment and contested judgment are different procedural outcomes. Preserve those distinctions when writing a partner assessment. Do not present an accusation as a finding or an awarded amount as collected cash.

Where available, examine later relevant orders and the current procedural status. If identity or outcome remains uncertain, say so. This is disciplined interpretation of the available record, not a reason to fill gaps with assumptions.

sections.heading: Fictional example: a similar cleaning-company name
paragraphs: A search returns a bankruptcy involving a contractor whose name resembles that of a proposed cleaning partner. The diligence lead initially places the result in the candidate’s file. Before attributing it, the team matches the actual legal entity and appropriate public identifiers.

If it is a different company, the similar name should not become an adverse conclusion about the candidate. If it is a match, the team reads the relevant documents and explains the status rather than relying on a search headline. Either way, state court coverage is still a separate task.

Use the linked Burgerim case guide as a reading exercise: identify its particular document type and then find what it does not establish about collection or later status. Do not transfer that case’s amounts or outcome into this candidate assessment. The reading habit is to separate identity, what a document records and the conclusion it can support.

seoTitle: Electronic FDD versus learning websites and course records

sections.heading: Separate understanding from the formal disclosure duty
paragraphs: An educational site explains questions and helps a team prepare information. The FDD must present prescribed disclosures and attached agreements in the required way. A case study, diagram, calculator or exported Expansion Brief does not become an FDD because it discusses the same business.

An FDD is information for a prospective franchisee, not government approval or a promise of profit. Likewise, a planning milestone is not legal permission to offer or sell. Keep the formal disclosure owner visible even where the sales process uses useful educational materials.

sections.heading: Electronic delivery does not permit every website feature
paragraphs: The prospect must be able to store, download, print or maintain the formal document. The rule permits specified navigation features in an electronic FDD, but restricts other multimedia, popups and links to external information (§ 436.6). Do not simply place disclosure paragraphs around an interactive website and assume the wrapper complies.

The product team and disclosure reviewer should examine the actual formal document and its features. A web format that works well for teaching can raise different questions when used for regulated disclosure.

sections.heading: Fictional example: a required training module
paragraphs: A brand wants prospects to finish a learning module before signing. The module explains recurring support costs and asks the reader to compare staffing scenarios. That may improve understanding, but completion does not show that the prospect received the current FDD and proposed agreements.

The team therefore maintains two records: learning progress and formal disclosure delivery. It checks the applicable waiting periods from the relevant documents and events, rather than from the moment a user completed the module. The educational tool can support the conversation without replacing the document-control process.

The two records can support the same commercial conversation without being interchangeable. Compare the actual electronic FDD’s permitted navigation and restricted features with the cited format rules; useful teaching multimedia does not become compliant disclosure merely because the subject matter overlaps. This exercise approves no website or delivery process.

paragraphs: The disclosure owner controls the current FDD, agreements, delivery method, receipts and retained versions. The product team maintains the explanatory website. Sales uses the reviewed formal timetable when arranging signatures and payments.

seoTitle: B2B franchise territories: national accounts and local costs

sections.heading: Make the territory promise specific
paragraphs: Item 12 requires disclosure of territory terms, exclusivity and its conditions, reserved channels and relevant competing operations. An exclusive territory does not promise protection from independent competitors. The disclosure and agreement should describe the intended arrangement consistently.

In practice, a cleaning or maintenance territory can overlap existing accounts, national buyers, online enquiries and jobs crossing boundaries. Geography alone cannot allocate all of those opportunities. The brand and operator need to understand what is reserved and which duties or conditions accompany their rights.

sections.heading: Separate the five account jobs
paragraphs: Ask who finds the customer, who has authority to bid and contract, who delivers each site’s service, who invoices and collects, and how income and costs are allocated. These jobs may sit with different entities. A centrally signed account can still require local staff, equipment and quality responsibility.

As business planning, test demand, delivery density and support capacity before a broad commitment. Staged development may reveal capacity before either party relies on a large territory. The enforceability of milestones and any non-waivable state protections require separate review.

sections.heading: Fictional example: a five-state request and one pilot
paragraphs: A Dutch maintenance operator asks for five states before completing one customer pilot. A potential customer wants one central agreement covering sites in several areas. The brand and candidate first map who will sell, deliver and bear travel, equipment and training costs at each site.

They then examine a staged commercial plan with documented milestones rather than treating the five-state label as proof of capability. If one operator cannot meet a national service obligation, the continuity and compensation questions must already have an owner. This illustration does not propose enforceable terms, decide state protections or promise freedom from independent competition.

For this additional fictional illustration only, suppose the brand wins and signs the central account and invoices the customer while a local operator performs one site’s work. The proposed allocation above is an optional commercial design, not a legal default or approved contract. Before promising exclusivity, compare the local delivery costs with the proposed income allocation and resolve continuity responsibilities. Item 12 disclosure, competition questions and non-waivable state protections remain separate.
